2d French Armored Division attached to the XV Corps (Third Army) at le Mans on 9 August 1944 (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 497). The end is an inferred value: no source read dates it. The XV Corps headquarters left Argentan eastward on 15 August with a skeleton staff left at Alencon for the holding operation of the French and 90th Divisions (p. 524), and the V Corps directed the division from its attack of 18 August (p. 533); the interval ends the day before, with the last row that lists it (13 August) as the earliest end.

2d French Armored Division under General Gerow's V Corps (First Army) on the southern shoulder of the Argentan-Falaise gap and for the liberation of Paris (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, pp. 533, 600). The kind is attached by analogy with the earlier XV Corps attachment; the source says under the control of. 2d French Armored Division with the XV Corps from 8 September 1944 (CMH The Lorraine Campaign, p. 185: it joined the XV Corps and took over the sector between Montargis and the Marne), under the Third Army and, from the transfer of the XV Corps on 29 September, under the Seventh Army (Riviera to the Rhine, p. 254). The kind is attached as in August. The end is the day before Patch transferred the division to the VI Corps on 27 November (Riviera to the Rhine, p. 454).

2d French Armored Division transferred by Patch from the XV Corps to the VI Corps on 27 November 1944 for the drive south from Strasbourg toward Selestat and Colmar (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 454). The end is an inferred value: no source read dates it. During the January 1945 German offensive the division returned to the XV Corps in the Sarre valley (p. 501) and was then moved south toward Strasbourg for the Colmar offensive (p. 535), but these moves are not dated in the pages read; the interval ends the day before the next row (8 February 1945), with the last row that lists it as the earliest end. The division was then attached to the French II Corps (p. 486), returned to the Seventh Army on 28 December (p. 496) and served with the XV Corps in January (p. 501), not with the VI Corps.

2d French Armored Division under the First French Army in the Colmar Pocket: Riviera to the Rhine, p. 559, says that for the moment de Lattre retained control of the French 2d Armored Division after the pocket was cleared. No source read dates the start, so valid_from is the date of the first row that lists it (8 February 1945, the link-up at Fessenheim). 2d French Armored Division under the Third Army from 9 August 1944: Patton gave the division to Haislip's XV Corps, to which it was attached at le Mans on 9 August (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 497). Kind unspecified_subordination: the division is a French formation under American command, and the source says only that Patton gave it to the corps. The end is an inferred value: no source read dates it; the interval ends the day before the first row under the First Army (18 August), with the last row that lists it (13 August) as the earliest end.

2d French Armored Division under the First Army through the V Corps for the closing of the Argentan-Falaise gap and the liberation of Paris (CMH Breakout and Pursuit, p. 600: eventually under the control of the First U.S. Army and the V Corps). 2d French Armored Division under the Third Army through the XV Corps from 8 September 1944 (CMH The Lorraine Campaign, p. 185) to 28 September, the day before the XV Corps passed to the 6th Army Group and the Seventh Army on 29 September (Riviera to the Rhine, p. 254). Kind unspecified_subordination as in August.

2d French Armored Division under the Seventh Army (6th Army Group) from 29 September 1944, when the XV Corps with the division passed to the 6th Army Group and the Seventh Army (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 254). The end is an inferred value: no source read dates it; the interval ends the day before the next row (8 February 1945, under the First French Army), with the last row that lists it (28 November 1944) as the earliest end. Kind unspecified_subordination as before. Army B under the direction of the American Seventh Army commander for the landings in southern France (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 28: Army B would remain under the direction of the American army commander). No source read dates the start, so valid_from is the date of the first row that lists it (20 August 1944, the attack on Toulon). Kind unspecified_subordination: the source says under the direction of.

After the activation of the 6th Army Group on 15 September 1944, Devers decided that Patch would continue to direct First French Army operations until the redeployment was completed, a situation that lasted only until 19 September (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 224). Kind operational_control for that direction of operations.

First French Army (Army B until its redesignation, 25 September 1944 in Wikipedia) under the 6th Army Group from 15 September 1944, when Headquarters, 6th Army Group, became operational and the French army became operationally, logistically and administratively independent of the Seventh Army (CMH Riviera to the Rhine, p. 224). Kind assigned: the army is one of the two armies of the army group. Open at the last row.

Kind assigned: a corps of the army. Open at the last row. Confirmed in the de Lattre pass: de Lattre, History of the French First Army, p. 123: "on the 1st September I entrusted it to General de Monsabert" (the 2nd Army Corps); valid_from unchanged.

French I Corps headquarters assembled at Aix-en-Provence on 1 September 1944 to command troops as a subordinate corps of the First Army (Wikipedia). Kind assigned: a corps of the army. Open at the last row. French 1st Armored Division under the I Corps of General Bethouart for the Belfort Gap offensive of November 1944 (Wikipedia: operating under the 1st Army Corps). No source read dates the start, so valid_from is the date of the first row that lists it; the source says operating under, so the kind is unspecified_subordination. Open at the last row.

The end is an inferred value: the interval ends the day before the next row (2 May 1945), which does not name a corps. Kind unspecified_subordination: the source says of the corps.

The directive of about 1 April that puts the division under direct Army orders until the I Corps enters (p. 429) is read in private notes without a firm day and is not used; the exact day the division left the I Corps is not stated, hence the range. Conflict kept, not resolved: the roadmap guess that the Karlsruhe rows point to the II Corps is partly supported, not refuted: the 6th Army Group plan of 28 March lets the II Corps force the Rhine with the 9th Colonial Division as a temporary passive flank (p. 421), and Monsabert (II Corps) orders the division to cross at Leimersheim on 30 March (p. 424); two lines of the private notes disagree on 2 to 3 April (p. 434: only the Bourgund group of the division stays with the II Corps until Karlsruhe falls; p. 435: the division stays in the II Corps under Directive No. 8). No II Corps relation is entered for 30 March to 2 April until pp. 421 to 436 are re-read (roadmap 352). After 2 April the Valluy group (the division with attached units) is temporary under the Army (p. 440), the division is again under Army orders on 17 April (p. 453) and the I Corps plan of 18 April lists it (p. 459); no relation is entered for those days, and the I Corps link from 18 April is left open (roadmap 352). Review (leftovers-1115, task b, roadmap 352, 15 November 2026, approved by Scott, t418u): valid_to old value 1945-04-02 (basis narrative); new value 1945-03-29 (basis inferred); valid_to_earliest unchanged (1945-02-09); start unchanged; reason: the de Lattre pass-2 notes (R686, paraphrase, the borrowed scan was not re-opened) show the division under the French II Corps, not the I Corps, in the days before 2 April: the 6th Army Group plan of 28-29 March counts it as the II Corps passive flank for the Rhine crossing (p. 421), Monsabert (II Corps) orders it to cross at Leimersheim on 30 March (p. 424), Directive No. 8 of 1 April gives the II Corps the Karlsruhe task with the division (p. 429) and Valluy has the task from 30 March (p. 430). The remnant left in the Wesel bridgehead came under the II Parachute Corps (C7937, B-262); Stacey p. 538 (C7571) has the division "put in from Army Group Reserve" at Bienen by 25 March, and CMH (C1183) has it counterattacking at Rees on 24 March, so the reserve status ended before then; the day is not documented (roadmap). The US XXI Corps under the French First Army from 23 January 1945: de Lattre, History of the French First Army, p. 359, has Devers telegraph at 03.35 on 23 January that the XXI Corps (Milburn), with its organic elements and the reinforced 75th US Division, is put under the French First Army immediately, and p. 365 has the corps command post set up at Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines on 26 January. The relationship is operational control, the kind taken from the corps being supplied by the US Seventh Army (p. 367); de Lattre does not date the end, and the CMH assignment table (CR0415) has the 75th Division under the French First Army to 10 February. Added in the de Lattre leftover pass, branch delattre-leftovers, 12 November 2026, approved by Scott: old value none (no relation), new value this relation. Review: small-fixes-1113, 13 November 2026: end date old value blank (end_unknown true, open_at_last_claim), new value still blank; no end date is entered. Reason: de Lattre (R686) still does not date the end (last operational mentions in early February; Milburn is decorated at Colmar on 11 February; Devers's Order of the Day of 10 February thanks the American 21st Army Corps). Riviera to the Rhine ch. 29 (R425) says only that 'by the end of February all major American participants in the Colmar struggle had returned north, including the XXI Corps', without a day. Wikipedia (R160) and the 71st Infantry Division association narrative (trailblazersww2.org, already weighed as secondary on CR0200) give 16 February 1945 as the return to Seventh Army, with a move to Morhange two days later. That day is not used: the official history gives no day, and the 12th Army Group situation map of 20 February (C5877) still shows the corps headquarters at Sainte-Croix-aux-Mines, next to the 26 January command post, which sits awkwardly with a completed move to Morhange on 18 February. Superseded on 14 November 2026 (see Review: cr1282-end below): the 6th Army Group G-3 Final Report (R453) dates the reversion. Review: cr1282-end, 14 November 2026, approved by Scott: end date old value blank (valid_to blank, valid_to_basis open_at_last_claim, end_unknown true); new value valid_to_earliest 1945-02-15, valid_to 1945-02-16, valid_to_basis narrative, end_unknown false (no end hour is documented). Reason: the Sixth Army Group G-3 Section Final Report (R453, page 43; a primary report, PDF copy at trailblazersww2.org) says: 'Regrouping of 6th Army Group commenced 15 February when 75th and 79th Infantry Divisions were released. XXI Corps reverted to control of Seventh Army and was given a sector on the left.' It does not give a separate day for the reversion, so 15 February is the earliest date. Three secondary sources give 16 February: Wikipedia (R160: attached to the French First Army from 25 January until 16 February 1945), the trailblazersww2.org XXI Corps history (R1166: 'returned to Seventh Army control on February 16th and moved to Morhange two days later'), and the bigpigeon.us ETO unit subordination page (R1167: French First Army 25 Jan, Seventh Army 16 Feb); they probably share one origin, so they count as one weaker family. The end is therefore between 15 and 16 February 1945 (valid_to_earliest 1945-02-15, valid_to 1945-02-16), the last day of the relation is 15 or 16 February, so it is certain through 15 February and possible on 16 February; neither day is chosen. The official history (Riviera to the Rhine ch. 29, R425) gives no day (end of February, all major American participants returned north) and de Lattre (R686) does not date the end; neither contradicts the range. Not resolved: the 12th Army Group situation map of 20 February (C5877) still shows the corps headquarters at Sainte-Croix-aux-Mines (a 0.3 map row, which can lag the move), whereas the XXI Corps history puts the move to Morhange on 18 February; C5877 is not changed. No new relation: the corps had been assigned to the US Seventh Army and 6th Army Group throughout (CR0201 and CR0200, from 27 December 1944), so the reversion is the end of this operational_control, not a new assignment.

A second family, Lodders and Kraandijk, '50 jaar regiment Stoottroepen', Militaire Spectator 163 (1994) no. 9 (R1162), records that Commando Limburg, by its direct relationship with the Americans, took increasing distance from Commando Zuid and Brabant (p. 405); the Limburg battalions were employed alongside the Americans from shortly after their formation and came under the Koninklijke landmacht section of Prince Bernhard's staff on 2 January 1945 (p. 406); the English employed Brabant companies as combat units at the front from 11 October 1944, and an English army commander delayed the Brabant transfer into the Koninklijke landmacht until May 1945 (Limburg had transferred in January; Commando Zuid was then abolished) (pp. 405-409). Other opened pages (Veteraneninstituut; stoottroepers.nl; English Wikipedia) are consistent with that split (Limburg under American command or embedded in the US Army; Brabant under British command, or belonging to 21st Army Group on the regimental site) but are not used to invent a formation-level relation. The Stoottroepen der Binnenlandse Strijdkrachten are the combat arm of the BS, organised in the split of the BS south of the great rivers on 22 September 1944 (de Jong, Het Koninkrijk, deel 10a, pp. 561-563, R894; NIMH, De oprichting van de Binnenlandse Strijdkrachten, R1163, as a second family). Kind administrative_control: the Stoottroepen are the combat arm of the BS (a component relationship). organic was considered, but organic relations are excluded from build/command_relations.csv and from who_controls, which is what this pass is meant to answer; administrative_control is the schema class for an administrative superior. HANDOFF describes administrative_control as temporary and ordinarily expecting an end; no end day is invented from the January/May transfers into the Koninklijke landmacht (R1162, month only) or from the 8 August 1945 dissolution of the BS (R1163), so the end stays open_at_last_claim. Start is the dated split (C9386), not the 18 September placement of six Eindhoven companies with XXX Corps (CR1285), when de Jong still called them stoottroepen of the OD. End left open at the last linked claim: the early May 1945 London return (C9388, de Jong pp. 757-758) still reports Stoottroepen (and Bewakingstroepen) as those arms in the liberated south. Lodders and Kraandijk (R1162) date the Limburg transfer into the Koninklijke landmacht in January 1945 and the Brabant transfer in May, after which Commando Zuid was abolished; NIMH (R1163) dates the dissolution of the BS as a whole to 8 August 1945. No end day is invented for this relation from those month-only or later dates. Review (branch small-fixes-1113, 14 November 2026, approved by Scott): old value none, new value this relation.

End, a documented range, conflict kept: the notes of p. 435 say that on the afternoon of 2 April de Lattre, seeing Monsabert's difficulty toward Pforzheim, takes the division under direct Army orders at once (earliest end, 2 April); the same page has Monsabert's Order No. 154, matching Directive No. 8, which keeps the division in the II Corps until Karlsruhe is captured (Directive No. 8 also says it then passes to direct Army control, p. 429-430), and Karlsruhe fell on the morning of 4 April (p. 436, C2042), when the western group under Valluy is separate from the II Corps group (p. 440); so the latest end is 4 April. The two readings are not reconciled without the page text. After the end: the division is under Army orders (Valluy group, p. 440); on 17 April it passes under Army orders (p. 453); the I Corps plan of 18 April lists it (p. 459); no relation is entered for those days (roadmap 352). The kind of subordination is not stated (unspecified_subordination). Start narrative and approximate ("etwa 11.3."). End, a range, two readings kept: B-453 pp. 6-7 has the division leave the II Parachute Corps for the LXXXVIII Corps about 26 March (C8010), so the last day with the II Parachute Corps would be 25 March (earliest end); FMS B-762 (Prittwitz, R810) German p. 2 has it pushed into the LXXXVIII Corps sector from the II Parachute Corps and placed under the corps between 30 March and 3 April (C7835), and on 3 April it goes with the corps to Armeegruppe Student (C7836), so the latest end is 2 April. Both are FMS manuscripts (one family), by the division commander and by the corps operations officer.
